What is the one-sentence rule I should tape to my monitor about splitting strings?

Here it is: never parse with split what has quoting rules.

Unpack it and it covers most of this territory. CSV fields quote commas. Shell commands quote spaces. JSON strings escape quotes and backslashes. URLs percent-encode almost anything. In every one of those formats, the separator character can legally appear inside a value, protected by the format's quoting or escaping mechanism — and split cannot see the protection, so it cuts through data and calls the pieces fields. The failure is silent and data-shaped: not an exception, but wrong values flowing downstream, discovered weeks later as a shifted column or a truncated name.

The contrapositive is equally useful: when a format has no quoting rules — a fixed-shape log line, your own key=value file with values that cannot contain the separator, a path on a system whose separator cannot appear in names — split and partition are not a guilty shortcut, they are the correct, proportionate tool. The skill is classifying the format before choosing, and noticing when a format grows quoting rules (they accrete in version two, when someone needs a comma in a name field).

And when the format does have quoting rules, the parser for it already exists in your standard library or ecosystem, written by someone who read the spec and survived the edge cases. Using it is not laziness. Reimplementing it badly, one bug report at a time, is the expensive kind of diligence.

Because normalization is lossy and opinions change, and those two facts together make stored-normalized data a one-way door.

Lossy first: every normalization step throws information away — the original capitalization, the spacing, whether the accent was composed or decomposed, the exact spelling the customer typed. Some of that information is legally or operationally the record (the name on the account is what the person wrote, not your casefolded version of it), and all of it is evidence when something later looks wrong. From raw data you can always produce any normalized form; from normalized data you can produce nothing else. Storage is forever and comparisons are cheap and repeated — keep the irreversible step on the repeatable side.

Opinions change second: your definition of "same" will be revised. You will add accent-stripping next year, or discover that collapsing internal spaces was wrong for product codes. If the stored data is raw, a rule change is a re-derivation — recompute the canonical column, re-run the dedupe, done. If you normalized at storage, the pre-change originals no longer exist, and the rule change is impossible rather than merely work. Teams discover this the first time a cleanup destroys the evidence needed to undo the cleanup.

The efficiency point is real but smaller than it looks, and it has a compatible answer: store the raw value and a derived canonical column beside it, computed at write time, recomputed whenever the rules change. You get indexed, fast comparisons and an intact original. The canonical column is a cache with a known recipe — and a cache can always be rebuilt from the source of truth. Normalize at compare time is the slogan; "the raw value is the source of truth, every normalized form is a rebuildable cache" is the practice.

A bug report says "the strip did not work" — the code calls s.strip() and the string keeps its spaces. I have seen this bug three times this year. Why does it keep happening?

arguments.code:
s = '  hello  '

s.strip()
print('after bare call:', repr(s))

s = s.strip()
print('after assignment:', repr(s))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
after bare call: '  hello  '
after assignment: 'hello'

Because strings are immutable: strip() cannot change s, so it returns a new string — and the bare call computes that new string and immediately throws it away. The original sits there untouched, wearing its spaces, while the code looks correct to every reader who skims it. It compiles, it runs, it does nothing. That combination — plausible appearance, zero effect — is why this bug recurs in every codebase and survives code review.

The same trap surrounds every string method: lower, replace, title, join's inputs, all of them return new strings. Python programmers learn "strings are immutable" as a trivia fact; this bug is what the fact means at 2 a.m. The related confusion is methods that do mutate — list.sort, list.append — which return None or nothing, so the mirror-image bug (x = items.sort(), now x is None) exists too. The two families have opposite contracts, and the language will not warn you about either mistake.

Defenses are habits, not tools. When a transformation "did not work," check the assignment before checking the transformation — it is the first suspect and takes five seconds to convict or clear. In review, any line that is a bare method call on a string, with the result unused, is guilty until proven innocent; linters can flag exactly this pattern (a statement with no effect). And when you teach this: do not say "strings are immutable" — say "every string method is a factory, not a mechanic; it hands you a new string, and if you do not take it, nothing happened."
Why do you insist on encoding="utf-8" every time I open a file? The default works on my machine.

Because "the default" is not a property of your code — it is a property of the machine, the OS, and the locale it happens to run under, and your code will eventually run somewhere it is different. Python's open() without an encoding uses locale.getpreferredencoding(False): on a typical Linux server that is UTF-8, on a Windows machine in the US it is often cp1252, in a minimal container or cron environment it can be ASCII. The same file, the same code: on your machine it reads fine; on the Windows box it mojibakes every accented character; under the ASCII locale it raises UnicodeDecodeError on the first é. "Works on my machine" is the exact signature of a default-encoding bug.

The explicit argument costs four seconds once and makes the file format a fact about the data rather than the environment. It also documents intent for the next reader: this file is UTF-8, full stop, and if bytes arrive that are not UTF-8 the error is immediate and attributable.

Two refinements complete the habit. For files whose encoding you do not control, name what you actually expect — utf-8-sig for vendor files that may carry a BOM (it behaves identically when no BOM is present), cp1252 for the legacy Windows export that really is cp1252 — and let the decode error, when it comes, point at the true assumption. And when writing CSV, pair encoding with newline='' so the csv module controls line endings. The meta-principle is the boundary rule from the decoding lesson: encodings are decided at the edges, explicitly, by you — or they are decided implicitly, differently, by every environment your code ever meets.
Search is failing our users: someone types "cafe" and gets no hits for documents titled "Café Menu", and typing "CAFÉ" misses "cafe hours". How do I make search match the way people mean?

arguments.code:
import unicodedata

def normalize_for_search(s):
    decomposed = unicodedata.normalize('NFD', s)
    without_marks = ''.join(c for c in decomposed if unicodedata.category(c) != 'Mn')
    return ' '.join(without_marks.casefold().split())

docs = ['Café Menu', 'cafe hours', 'The CAFÉ Terrace', 'Tea Room']

index = [(doc, normalize_for_search(doc)) for doc in docs]

for query in ['cafe', 'CAFÉ', 'café terrace']:
    q = normalize_for_search(query)
    hits = [doc for doc, norm in index if q in norm]
    print(repr(query), '->', hits)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
'cafe' -> ['Café Menu', 'cafe hours', 'The CAFÉ Terrace']
'CAFÉ' -> ['Café Menu', 'cafe hours', 'The CAFÉ Terrace']
'café terrace' -> ['The CAFÉ Terrace']

The fix is one normalization function, applied identically to both sides of the search. Each document is indexed under its normalized form — accents stripped by the NFD-and-drop-marks trick, case folded, whitespace collapsed — and each query is put through the exact same pipeline before matching. "cafe" now matches all three café documents because both sides meet at the canonical form cafe; "CAFÉ" as a query normalizes to cafe too, so the shouty typing finds the quiet document; and the original titles are what get displayed, because the normalized form is an index key, never a replacement.

This record is the batch in miniature, so notice how many earlier lessons are load-bearing inside six lines: normalization before comparison (the NFC lesson, here in its NFD working clothes), casefold rather than lower for matching, whitespace collapsing for sloppy input, and store-raw/derive-for-comparison as the architecture. Search quality, in text systems, is mostly normalization quality.

The limits are the ones you would predict. Accent-stripping is a language policy: it declares café and cafe the same, which is right for a café menu and wrong for a system where ñ and n distinguish words (año/ano is the famous Spanish minimal pair). Substring matching after normalization still cannot rank, stem (run versus running), or forgive typos — those are the next layers (tokenization, stemming, edit distance), each with its own policy decisions. Build them in this order and each layer stays debuggable: normalize, tokenize, then get clever.
My codebase is full of "stringly-typed" data — dates, amounts, booleans, all strings, parsed over and over in different places. What is the way out?

Parse once, at the edge, into real types — and let the interior of the program never see the strings.

The stringly-typed tax is paid in four currencies. Repeated parsing: twelve places each strptime the same field, each with its own format string, and they drift until two parts of the system disagree about what the text means. Invalid states everywhere: a string can be "2026-13-45" or "amount: banana" in a way a date or an int cannot, so every consumer defends itself, or fails to. Silent wrong comparisons: "10" < "9" as strings, "1.0" != "1.00", and the boolean special — the string 'False' is truthy, so a config value read as text makes `if flag:` take the true branch for a flag that says False. That one has bitten every Python programmer who reads config from the environment, where everything is a string by law. And no help from tools: a date object offers .weekday() and arithmetic; a date-shaped string offers slicing and hope.

The migration does not need a rewrite. Pick the boundary where text enters (request handler, file reader, environment loader) and add a parse step there that produces a small typed record — a dataclass with date, int-cents, and bool fields — converting with parsers that raise named errors on garbage. Interior functions change their signatures to take the record; the compiler-equivalent (your tests, your type checker if you run one) finds the consumers still expecting strings. Fields nobody has typed yet can ride along as raw strings inside the record, explicitly marked, to be evicted one by one.

The end state is the "parse, don't validate" architecture: by the time data reaches business logic, it is incapable of being malformed in shape, and the only checks left inside are business truths (sufficient balance, within opening hours) rather than text archaeology.

Counting lines in a file keeps giving me one extra when the file ends with a newline. And Windows files leave a stray character at the end of each line. Are splitlines and split("\n") really different?

arguments.code:
s = 'a\nb\n'

print("split('\\n'):", s.split('\n'), '-> len', len(s.split('\n')))
print('splitlines:', s.splitlines(), '-> len', len(s.splitlines()))

win = 'a\r\nb\r\n'
print("windows split('\\n'):", win.split('\n'))
print('windows splitlines:', win.splitlines())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
split('\n'): ['a', 'b', ''] -> len 3
splitlines: ['a', 'b'] -> len 2
windows split('\n'): ['a\r', 'b\r', '']
windows splitlines: ['a', 'b']

They differ in both of the ways biting you.

The trailing-newline phantom: 'a\nb\n' contains two lines, but split('\n') treats the newline as a separator between fields, so a trailing newline manufactures a third, empty field — your count of 3 for a 2-line file. splitlines() treats newlines as line terminators, which matches how humans and editors count: two lines, no phantom. Any time you count, iterate, or validate lines, the terminator model is the one you mean.

The Windows residue: split('\n') on CRLF text leaves the \r attached to every line ('a\r'), where it poisons comparisons, lengths, and anything downstream that prints it invisibly. splitlines() understands \r\n as a single boundary — and also lone \r, and several Unicode line boundaries — so the lines come out clean regardless of which system wrote the file.

Two honest caveats. splitlines also splits on characters you may not expect (vertical tab, form feed, U+2028), which inside a single field of data could surprise you; for machine formats with an exact spec, that breadth is a reason to read the spec rather than improvise. And for actually reading files, the file object itself iterates lines correctly — text.splitlines is for text already in memory. But as a rule: lines are splitlines' job. split('\n') is for the rare case where the empty trailing field is itself meaningful data, and you should be able to say why before using it.
Give me a checklist I can use when reviewing code that handles text — the questions that catch the bugs this whole area is famous for.

Work through these in order; each one is a bug family with a body count.

Entry. Where does this text come from, and what was done to it at the boundary? Bytes should be decoded once, explicitly (encoding named, not defaulted), and external text should pass one documented normalization point. If decoding or cleaning happens in five places, that is the finding.

Levels. For every length, limit, slice, and truncation: is this rule about bytes, code points, grapheme clusters, or display width — and is the code measuring that level? A byte-limited column checked with len, a user-facing character limit enforced in bytes, a table padded without width awareness: level confusions, all.

Parsing. Is anything being split that has quoting rules (CSV, shell, JSON, URLs)? Is a format with internal validity (dates, versions, amounts) being checked by shape alone instead of parsed into its type? Is malformed input reported with position and content, or silently skipped?

Comparison. Are compared strings canonicalized — identically, on both sides, by one named function? Are values being compared as text when a parsed type exists? Is fuzzy matching anywhere near a decision with consequences, without a human in the loop?

Cleaning. Does any cleanup destroy data this field needs (leading zeros, case, accents, internal spacing)? Is raw text preserved anywhere, or did the cleaned version replace it? Do strip-family calls pass multi-character arguments (the set-not-substring trap)? Are string method results always assigned (the immutability trap)?

Exit. Is user text escaped per output context — HTML by the template engine, CSV by the writer, JSON by dumps, SQL by parameters — or is anything being concatenated into a language by hand?

A review that asks these six families of questions will catch nearly every text bug that experience teaches — the point of the checklist is that you should not need the experience personally, one production incident at a time.
